title: Ping-Pong, PE, and the Rise and Fall of Canvas
author: Rob Nelson
summary: Rob Nelson uses the history of Canvas and its maker Instructure to explain why so much digital infrastructure seems to be failing. He recalls choosing a learning management system in 2011 and 2014, when a venture-backed startup looked like a healthy alternative to the stagnant incumbent Blackboard and the collapsing open-source consortium behind Sakai. He then traces how leveraged buyouts and private equity turned Instructure, like Blackboard before it, into an asset passed between public and private capital. The evidence is a list of recent product failures, including unwanted emojis, a broken gradebook, AI upselling and a ransom-paid data breach in May 2026. Nelson rebuts the industry defense that speed and standardization are simply the price of scale, and argues the competitive market he once trusted no longer exists. The piece moves from diagnosis to a local call to action, urging teachers and students to press campus decision makers on platform contracts and AI together.
points: Canvas followed Blackboard into a cycle of private equity ownership, cost cutting and public offerings that rewards extracting value over serving schools.
Recent Canvas failures, from uncontrollable emojis to the 2026 breach, show a move-fast ethos that shifts testing and security costs onto institutions.
The startup-disrupts-incumbent story no longer holds because founders and incumbents draw on the same giant pools of capital and many hope AI displaces human labor.
Decisions about AI and decisions about digital platforms are entangled, so campuses should address them together and ask about contracts, open source and open weight models.
Nelson recommends preparing for worse products, keeping a plan B for moving platforms, and practicing pluralism in how teachers use digital tools.
quotes: Blackboard, acting as incumbents often do, ignored the pressure to update its product. Sakai, acting as non-profit consortia often do, fell apart amid political infighting as some institutions withdrew to do their own thing.

Leveraged buyouts (LBOs) and private equity (PE) are a set of legal and accounting mechanisms used by wealthy people to extract money from money from public companies. For the financial and legal professionals and their rich clients, this is a very profitable game where a public company is bought by outsiders who use the corporation’s own debt to finance the purchase.

Moving fast and breaking things is a strategy for transferring the cost of developing new features or protecting sensitive data to institutions and customers. When disaster strikes because a feature release wasn’t thoroughly tested or experienced developers have been fired, the corporate communication team is ready with anodyne statements designed to deflect attention until the crisis is over.

The system is not well-functioning, nor is it competitive. These days all the founders are playing the same game as the incumbent CEOs, and many of them hope AI disrupts public education right out of existence. They don’t say it anymore because they found out it does not poll well, but their aspirations are for AI to disrupt all human labor. Two startups, Anthropic and OpenAI, and a few old ones like Facebook and Google, that became megacorporations are moving fast to build machines that replace people and break digital systems.

Instructure is a paddle that is used by both the public and the private sides of the capital markets game. Any startup that has a decent shot at success gets funded by the same giant reservoirs of capital that flow through Silicon Valley giants. A paddle is a paddle, whether it is in private or public hands. Schools and colleges, hospitals and youth sports leagues, people and their old systems, just get ping-ponged around the table.

Talk to them about the decisions your institutions needs to make, and not just about AI. Digital technologies are all deeply entangled, a messy complex of solutions and problems born of networked, electronic computers, huge amounts of data, and half-understood advances in computer science. Every decision about AI on your campus is directly related to to choices made about the digital platforms in use, and vice versa.

Understand how the incentives of the software industry and the role that private equity will lead to digital technology products getting worse over time. Broken public markets means campuses need to constantly evaluate whether the costs to switch are worth paying and what options are available. What’s that evaluation process at your institution? Who is exploring alternatives?

Yet, I believe that large AI models are learning systems that we do not yet understand how to use well or safely. If that’s true, then they are too important to leave in the hands of people running startups. Better to bring the development of this technology into public institutions designed for research and teaching. Research universities are much safer environments for inquiry into and testing dangerous technology. After all, they’re the ones with laboratories for studying viruses and nuclear energy.
context: Nelson shows that both the incumbent and the consortium failed at the same moment, which is what created the opening Canvas filled.
He defines leveraged buyouts plainly as a financial technology that extracts money from companies using their own debt.
He argues that the industry's speed rhetoric is a cost transfer that leaves institutions to absorb the damage from untested releases.
This passage supports his claim that the 2014 faith in startup competition was misplaced because the market now serves the same capital and the same AI ambitions.
The paddle image recasts Instructure as a tool of the capital markets, so schools and other institutions are the ones being batted around.
He ties platform governance to AI decisions, which is why he wants campus conversations to cover the whole digital stack.
This is the first of his practical suggestions, and it asks institutions to assume decline and keep switching options open.
His closing argument is that powerful AI belongs in public research institutions that already handle dangerous inquiry safely.
